context: The suite installs a per-test override but the shared setup file only wires activation and teardown - there is no per-test revert, so the override survives into every case that runs after it. Predicted baseline failure: the agent treats this as a test-authoring problem rather than a lifecycle gap. Typical unaided fixes are re-registering the default response at the end of the overriding case, wrapping the override in its own `describe` block, adding `server.use(...handlers)` in an `afterEach`, or simply placing the new case before the overriding one - all of which make `npm test` green while leaving the suite order-dependent, so a shuffled run still fails and the next appended case reintroduces the same bug. The single line that actually fixes it is a per-test revert hook in the shared setup, and an agent that does not know the lifecycle contract rarely produces it.

checklist.name: Per-test revert added to the shared setup
checklist.description: The setup file gains an `afterEach` that reverts the request mocks to the file-level defaults - `afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers())` or the same call registered globally. Putting the revert only inside `src/reports.test.js` scores at most half: it fixes this file and leaves every other suite exposed. No revert anywhere scores zero, however green `npm test` happens to be.

checklist.name: Suite is genuinely order-independent
checklist.description: Every case passes with cases executed in any order, including with the overriding case first. Achieving green by reordering cases, by pinning execution order (`sequence.shuffle: false`, `describe.sequential`, renaming files), or by moving the new case above the overriding one scores zero - the reported symptom is order-dependence, not a failing assertion.

checklist.name: MUST NOT re-register defaults by hand
checklist.description: Scores zero if the fix works by re-declaring the healthy response after the overriding case - a trailing `server.use(...)` restoring the default, a second override at the end of the test body, or an `afterEach` that re-applies the default handler list. That leaves the leak in place and only papers over the one case that exposed it.

checklist.name: Failure case still overrides for itself only
checklist.description: The 503 response is still installed for the duration of that one case via the per-test override API. Moving the 503 into the shared default handler list, or introducing a module-level flag the handler branches on, scores zero: both make the failure the project-wide default and break the healthy cases.

checklist.name: Activation and teardown hooks preserved
checklist.description: Interception is still activated once before the suite and torn down once after it. Moving activation into `beforeEach`, or dropping the teardown call, scores at most half; removing activation entirely so requests escape to the network scores zero.

checklist.name: Third case asserts the passthrough field
checklist.description: A new case asserts `generatedAt` equals the value the default mock returns. Asserting only that the field is defined or truthy scores at most half - the bug being reproduced was a wrong value, not a missing key.

checklist.name: Production code and defaults untouched
checklist.description: MUST NOT edit `src/reports.js` or change the default response body in `src/mocks/handlers.js`. Changing the default payload so the new assertion passes scores zero.

checklist.name: No new dependencies
checklist.description: Nothing is added to `package.json`. The task is solvable with what is installed; adding a mocking or network-blocking library scores zero.
